system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-04-14 22:54:00 to 2169-04-25 14:12:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of epigastric pain three months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. She reported nausea, one episode of non-bloody vomiting, and looser stools. A CT scan revealed oral contrast in both the gastric pouch and remnant stomach, suggesting a fistulous connection, along with mild dilatation of the proximal efferent limb. An EGD confirmed two perianastomotic ulcers on the jejunal side with no active bleeding, and an H. pylori serology test was negative. She was managed with IV Protonix and pain control using IV morphine, later transitioned to oral omeprazole and Roxicet. Her diet was advanced from clear liquids to bariatric stage III, with a switch to lactose-free to address diarrhea. She tolerated oral intake and medications well, with controlled pain and stable vitals, leading to discharge home with follow-up instructions and a two-week surgical clinic appointment.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

Brief Hospital Course:
Mrs. ___ presented to the Emergency Department the evening of 
___ with weakness following 7 days of inability to 
tolerate solids or liquids due to ongoing nausea.  Intravenous 
fluids, vitamins and electrolytes were administered and the 
patient was transferred to the general surgical ward for further 
management.

On hospital day #1 the patient continued to have epigastric pain 
and nausea which was managed with intravenous ondansetron.  
Intravenous pantoprazole was also resumed due to known 
ulcerations at the gastrojejunostomy, which was diagnosed on her 
previous admission.  

On hospital day #2 the epigastric pain improved significantly, 
but the nausea persisted.  Sucralfate therapy was initiated at 
this time.  On hospital day #3 the patient began having 
diarrhea.  Stool cultures were sent and intravenous fluids were 
resumed.  The following day stool cultures were negative for 
ova, parasites and campylobacter but positive clostridium 
difficile.  Oral metronidazole therapy was initiated.  

On hospital day #5 the patient was experiencing persistent 
diarrhea, therefore, Infectious Disease was consulted for 
recommendations regarding optimal managment of clostridium 
difficile in this patient.  They recommended continued oral 
metronidazole treatment for an initial 14-day period with 
potential for a longer treatment course given daily PPI 
requirments.  

As the hospital course progressed, the patient's diarrhea 
improved significantly.  Her nausea and epigastric pain 
completely resolved and she was able to ingest adequate amounts 
of protein, calories and fluids.

At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
with stable vital signs.  The patient was tolerating a stage 3 
diet, ambulating, voiding without assistance, and without pain.  
The patient received discharge teaching and follow-up 
instructions with understanding verbalized and agreement with 
the discharge plan.

Discharge Instructions: Please call your surgeon or return to 
the emergency department if you develop a fever greater than 
101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, 
pain unrelieved by your pain medication, severe nausea or 
vomiting, severe abdominal bloating, inability to eat or drink, 
foul smelling or colorful drainage from your incisions, redness 
or swelling around your incisions, or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.

Diet: Stay on Stage III diet until your follow up appointment. 
Do not self advance
diet, do not drink out of a straw or chew gum.

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are being discharged on medications to treat the pain 
from your operation. These medications will make you drowsy and 
impair your ability to drive a motor vehicle or operate 
machinery safely. You MUST refrain from such activities while 
taking these medications.
2. You should begin taking a chewable complete multivitamin with 
minerals. No gummy vitamins.
3. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling weak and nauseous. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had nausea for about a week now and I can’t keep anything down—not even water. I felt so weak today I knew I had to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were here recently for epigastric pain and a marginal ulcer after your gastric bypass, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was on omeprazole and it was helping, but then the nausea came back and I couldn’t eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll start by giving you IV fluids to rehydrate you. We’ll also continue the proton pump inhibitor through the IV to protect your stomach lining, since you have a history of ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon? I’m really worried about not getting enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Right now, we need to control the nausea. We’re giving you ondansetron for that. Once you’re stable, we’ll try small sips and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any change in the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, I think. The pain in my stomach is less, but I still feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to add a medication called sucralfate. It coats the ulcer and helps it heal. You’ll take it four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the nausea still related to the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’re also watching for other causes. We’ll keep monitoring you and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have some news. You started having diarrhea yesterday, so we sent a stool sample. It came back positive for C. diff—Clostridium difficile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff? Is that serious? How did I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an infection that can happen after antibiotics or in hospital settings. It’s treatable. We’re starting you on metronidazole, an antibiotic that targets C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, over the next few days. We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now and monitor your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea is still ongoing, so we consulted Infectious Disease. They agree with continuing metronidazole for a full 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because I’m on the omeprazole? I heard that can increase the risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right—PPIs can increase the risk of C. diff. But we still need to protect your stomach from ulcers, so we’ll continue it with caution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your diarrhea has improved a lot since yesterday. That’s a sign the metronidazole is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can finally catch my breath. Can I try eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids and advance slowly to your stage 3 bariatric diet. Small, frequent meals—no straws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time—no straws, no gum. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Nausea is gone, and you’re tolerating solids. Your labs are stable, and you’re well-hydrated now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re heading that way. We’ll make sure you’re on the right medications and have a clear plan before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on your discharge plan. You’ll continue omeprazole twice a day, sucralfate four times a day, and metronidazole three times a day for six more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to crush all my pills, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And stick to chewable vitamins—no gummies. We’re also adjusting your vitamin D dose to 1,000 units daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re up and walking, eating well, and your symptoms are resolved. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up a follow-up with your surgeon. In the meantime, avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to acetaminophen if I need pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, no heavy lifting for six weeks. You can do light exercise, but avoid anything that strains your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy. What about my CPAP? Should I keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Continue your CPAP at night. It’s important for your breathing and overall recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your labs are normal, you’re afebrile, and you’ve had no pain or nausea. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like a new person.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over your discharge instructions one more time to make sure everything is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is your last day. You’re tolerating your stage 3 diet, walking independently, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What symptoms should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or go to the ER if you develop a fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking the metronidazole until it’s all gone, even after I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finish the full course. It’s important to prevent the infection from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll follow up with my surgeon in two weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll assess your progress and adjust your long-term plan if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Just take it slow at home and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions before we wrap up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I should crush all pills, stay on the stage 3 diet, and avoid NSAIDs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. And continue your vitamins and sucralfate as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel off, I should call the surgeon or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Better safe than sorry. We want you to recover fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I restart all my previous medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, except we’ve adjusted your vitamin D and omeprazole. The rest stay the same—just crush them before taking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll double-check the list you gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. And remember, no straws or gum—it can cause bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Just follow the plan and you’ll do fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. I’ve missed my bed!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I bet. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll start packing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call your name when it’s time to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with nausea, weakness, and inability to tolerate oral intake one week after a prior discharge for a marginal ulcer following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She was dehydrated and started on IV fluids and IV pantoprazole for ulcer protection. On hospital day 3, she developed diarrhea, and stool testing confirmed Clostridium difficile infection. Oral metronidazole was initiated, and Infectious Disease recommended a 14-day course. Sucralfate was added for ulcer coating. Her symptoms resolved over the course of the admission, and she advanced to a stage 3 bariatric diet. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue omeprazole, sucralfate, metronidazole, and crushed oral medications, with follow-up in the surgical clinic.
problems: Intestinal infection due to Clostridium difficile
